text: I am comparing Q’s incentive-compatible mechanisms with P’s measured review protocols. Initial candidate: treat reviewer/critic reports and stopping as a mechanism with costly verification and correlated errors; check whether Q’s obedience and truth-telling conditions expose a testable failure mode in P’s consensus rule. I will ground this in both papers before endorsing it.

I am checking whether Q\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s weak-monitor or peer-discipline mechanism can explain P\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s reviewer--critic failure and yield a testable design. P reports false agreement and recovery with evidence-required disagreement (P, lines 281--363); Q models biased weak monitors and reports/rewards (Q, Sections 4--5). I will inspect the exact assumptions before claiming a transfer.

Q, Example “Peer discipline” (inputs/Q.tex lines 1645–1736) proves support-wise implementation of any feasible rule only if each pair of supported types has distinct beliefs about co-player types (condition S), with a large quadratic peer score and a reward term canceling reported utility. Q explicitly notes partial rather than full implementation near lines 425–431. P, SWE-PRBench lines 281–365, reports naive AR F1 (0.457), below single reviewer (0.495), and documents a critic yielding to a reviewer despite a manually verified concern; evidence-constrained disagreement raises F1 to (0.533). Hypothesis to test: peer agreement is not an independent certificate of correctness when model errors or incentives are shared. I am checking whether Q’s separation, reward, and verifiability premises can be instantiated for P.

Alternative to peer scoring: Q\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s weak-to-strong oversight already proves a monitor-optimal instrument can harm the human. In Q, Regime III lets monitor (W) select reward (r_b^{III}(a)=-2(b-w)a), inducing (a=\theta+w), so (L_W^{III}=0) while (L_H^{III}=w^2) (Q lines 2099--2180); Q explicitly says expanding monitor discretion need not improve human payoff (lines 2178--2187). P\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s critic can likewise reach agreement while dropping a manually verified bug (P lines 314--337), and its constrained three-verdict menu raises review F1 from (0.457) to (0.533) (P lines 281--365). This is an analogy, not an application of Q\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s quadratic theorem: P has no demonstrated stable utility, reward schedule, or verifiable citation. I am probing a sharp, testable condition under which evidence gating beats free-form consensus.

The Q-to-P transfer is conditional, not demonstrated. Q’s peer result assumes a known map from private types to distinct conditional beliefs over co-player types, plus unbounded enforceable rewards and (-\infty) action penalties (Q lines 1653–1736). P’s R/C are prompt roles of the same Sonnet 4.5 model (P lines 108–116), with no scored reports or measured type-belief map; same model alone does not imply Q’s separation condition fails. P’s text-constraint improvement to F1 (0.533) was measured on review-only SWE-PRBench (P lines 338–365); its SWE-bench Verified result (75.2\%\) uses a different skills-form protocol (P lines 370–409). A valid study must estimate conditional judgment distributions and test an actual reward/audit intervention, not call AR an implementation of Q’s theorem.

I sharpen the pair question to: when does verifiable, preserved dissent improve reviewer--critic oversight, rather than merely produce agreement? A minimal review-flag model gives a measurable threshold. Let \(\pi\) be true-bug prevalence, \(t\) baseline true-positive rate, \(f\) baseline false-positive rate. If an evidence gate retains fractions \(s\) of true flags and \(z\) of false flags, then \(F_1^{\rm base}=2\pi t/[\pi(1+t)+(1-\pi)f]\), and \(F_1^{\rm gate}=2\pi ts/[\pi(1+ts)+(1-\pi)fz]\). Algebra: gate helps exactly when \((1-\pi)f(s-z)>\pi(1-s)\). A merely printable citation with \(s=z<1\) worsens F1; semantic verification must discriminate sufficiently to offset lost true flags. This is a proposed model of flag filtering, not a theorem about P\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s full iterative protocol, which can also add flags. Q\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s hard-evidence order (Q lines 299--310) motivates measuring \(s-z\); P\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s appendix prompts (P lines 1130--1217) demand citations but do not verify semantic entailment.

Important limit on my weak-monitor analogy: Q\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s robust first-best result (Proposition 12, Q lines 2190--2228) uses an enforceable menu of reward schedules, extreme off-target actions, a bound on monitor bias, and a perfectly state-informed actor. P\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s text-only instructions supply none of these. Q also explicitly proves only partial implementation as an equilibrium and leaves full implementation/collusion open (Q lines 425--431). Thus P\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s (0.533) F1 should motivate an audited evidence mechanism and a randomized test, not be cited as Q\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s theorem in action.

Correction to my preceding entry: cite Q\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s named proposition “Robust first best” (\(\mathtt{prop:optimal-oversight}\)), not “Proposition 12”; the source label is reliable, and I did not verify a printed proposition number.

Cross-check of P\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s intervention: it is a bundle, not an isolated hard-evidence test. The changed reviewer prompt says that on AGREE it must keep all flags and on any verdict incorporate a missed bug (P lines 1152--1172); the changed critic prompt introduces three verdict labels and requests citations (P lines 1185--1233). The F1 gain on the same 100 PRs (P lines 281--359) therefore cannot identify whether preservation, verdict taxonomy, citation syntax, or semantic evidence caused the gain. Also P\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s judge matches human comments, which can reject valid unmatched findings (P lines 680--688). A publishable test should randomize these components on held-out PRs, assess citation entailment with blinded human adjudication, and measure both matched-comment F1 and true defect outcomes. Prediction from my threshold model is benefit only where evidence discrimination \(s-z\) is large enough relative to lost true flags; uncertain/contextual bugs can reverse it.

Best candidate publication line: a verifiability-aware reviewer--critic protocol, with a theory-guided experiment. Q\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s hard evidence means certificates can be withheld but not counterfeited (Q lines 299--303), and its weak-monitor analysis says monitor-optimal control can worsen the human\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s outcome (Q lines 2178--2185). P observes both false-positive accumulation and loss of a true dissenting concern under a consensus-seeking critic (P lines 314--336), then improves review F1 using three text verdicts (P lines 338--359), but prompt citations are not checked as certificates (P lines 1138--1217). Proposed study: freeze initial R/C judgments before dialogue, separately randomize verdict taxonomy, dissent preservation, citation requirement, and independent semantic verification; adjudicate cited code and actual bugs blindly; compare false consensus, precision/recall/F1, patch success, and tokens on held-out PRs. The simple filtering condition in entry 6 gives a preregisterable sign prediction, with \(s\) and \(z\) estimated from adjudicated traces. No result yet shows this works: semantic verification may miss context-dependent bugs, and Q\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s preference/reward/equilibrium assumptions do not hold automatically for P. P\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s improved review-only protocol was not the one tested for SWE-bench patch success (P lines 370--409). This is a concrete research program, not a novelty or performance claim.

Independent alternative to an evidence gate: preserve *blind initial* reviewer/critic judgments and test epistemic separation before they converse. In Q’s quadratic peer score (Q lines 1670–1735), a truthful binary signal type (t) beats false report (hat t) in expected score by (\Lambda\|\beta_t-\beta_{\hat t}\|_2^2). If an added conformity/effort motive can gain at most (B), truthful reporting is a best response when (\Lambda\delta\geq B), where (\delta=\min_{t\ne\hat t}\|\beta_t-\beta_{\hat t}\|_2^2); if (\delta=0) and a false report strictly gains from conformity, scaling this peer score cannot fix it. This is a direct specialization of Q’s proof, not a new theorem. P’s two independent reviewers (P lines 136–143, 281–311) do not measure this predictive separation, and blind initial judgments could be scored before AR’s convergence. Proposed study: elicit initial bug judgments and peer forecasts, estimate separation on training PRs, compare blind peer-scored reports, ordinary AR, and evidence-constrained AR on held-out PRs, including transition-specific false approvals. Peer scores elicit informative signals only under Q’s behavioral assumptions; they do not themselves verify code correctness.

I checked emmy\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s entry 11 against Q\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s proof: it defines \(\delta\) as the minimum squared distance between conditional co-player-report distributions and chooses score weight at least \(M/\delta\) (Q lines 1697--1735), so the stated \(B/\delta\) extension is sound if \(B\) really bounds other gains. This is complementary to evidence verification: peer forecasts can make initial reports incentive-compatible under separation, while an independent semantic checker tests whether a cited code span actually supports a bug claim. For an AR study, “blind initial critic” must mean an independently elicited initial bug judgment before the critic sees R\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s review; P\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s critic as written sees R\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s review (P lines 1205--1213). Neither condition has been measured in P.

My peer-score alternative has a sharper limitation: Q’s separation condition tests whether types predict peers differently, not whether those types predict the true bug state. Counterexample: let true bug state (Y\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/2)), and both reviewers observe the same independent nuisance bit (Z\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/2)); set private type (t_i=Z). Then (\beta_i[0]) and (\beta_i[1]) are opposite point masses, so Q’s squared separation is (\delta=2), the maximum for binary peer types, and its score can elicit (Z) strictly. Yet (I(Y;t_1,t_2)=0), so no decision based on these reports beats the prior Bayes decision. This formal counterexample is my synthesis, not a claim in Q/P. Thus estimated peer separation alone cannot certify review quality; the study must also test conditional defect informativeness against independently adjudicated outcomes. It supports Ada’s insistence on a separate semantic-verification arm, while warning that high reviewer agreement can reflect shared nuisance cues.

Prior-work check narrows the claim. I searched “peer prediction correlated errors shared model failure truthful elicitation LLM paper”, “peer prediction spot checks audit ground truth proper scoring correlated signals mechanism design paper”, and “LLM code review executable evidence failing test witness review findings study”. Peer-score training for LLM truthfulness already exists: https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.20299 (also cited by Q near lines 1780–1789); spot-checking with limited ground truth is established: https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/11336 and https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.07042; a code-review verification filter using executable counterfactual evidence also exists: https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00539. A publication would need a specific new result about sequential reviewer–critic convergence, measured peer-signal informativeness versus defect informativeness, and the effect of preserving blind dissent or verified witnesses. I found prior work, so make no novelty claim for scoring, audits, or executable checks alone.

Best supported joint line: separate *eliciting a private review signal* from *learning whether the patch is defective*. Q’s peer-discipline proposition (Q lines 1653–1736) gives truth-telling under distinct co-player-belief maps and large enforceable rewards, but only support-wise/partial implementation; my #14 counterexample shows perfect peer separation can coexist with zero bug information. P’s naive AR review F1 (0.457) and critic-yields-to-reviewer case (P lines 281–336) expose a sequential consensus failure; text-constrained AR reaches (0.533) on the review-only task (P lines 338–365), yet the intervention bundles multiple prompt changes and gives no hard certificate (P lines 1122–1233). Sharpened publication question: after independent initial reviews, can a mechanism that preserves dissent and selectively verifies *semantic* evidence reduce false consensus at fixed token/audit cost, especially when peers are mutually predictable but wrong? Discriminating experiment: randomize blind-initial-report preservation, peer forecast scoring, and independent witness/audit checks on held-out PRs; estimate both conditional peer-report separation and information about adjudicated defects, transitions from true dissent to false agreement, precision/recall, patch success, and cost. Require a behavioral/incentive model if claiming Q-style implementation. No present result proves this intervention helps; prior work already covers generic peer scoring, spot checks, and executable code verification (URLs in #15). Unresolved: whether enough code-review findings admit sound cheap witnesses, whether LLM behavior responds to enforceable rewards, and whether gains survive on repository repair rather than review-only F1.
ready at #16

I checked emmy\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s nuisance-bit counterexample in entry 14 against Q: if \(t_1=t_2=Z\) with \(Z\perp Y\), then \(\beta[0]=(1,0)\), \(\beta[1]=(0,1)\), so \(\delta=2\) in Q\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s peer score (Q lines 1653--1734), while \(I(Y;t_1,t_2)=0\). Thus even maximal type separation can reward perfectly reported, perfectly useless review signals. The useful distinction is between report fidelity and bug informativeness. A sequential AR experiment needs independent initial judgments, transition traces, and blinded defect adjudication; P\(\text{\textquotesingle}\)s final matched-comment F1 alone cannot identify which stage changed either property (P lines 270--273, 328--359). This endorses the counterexample and narrows the main line to preserving and checking defect evidence rather than peer agreement alone.
ready at #18

Cross-checking Ada #18 yields a two-way separation. In Q, condition (S) distinguishes conditional beliefs over peer types, not predictive value for the task state (Q lines 1653–1734). My #14 example has maximal peer separation \(\delta=2\) but no bug information. Conversely, let \(Y\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/2)\), reviewer type \(t_1=Y\), and critic type \(t_2\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/2)\) independently. Then \(\beta_1[0]=\beta_1[1]=(1/2,1/2)\), so Q peer separation fails, although \(t_1\) perfectly predicts \(Y\). These are counterexamples within the type-belief abstraction, not claims about P data or impossibility of other mechanisms. Thus peer predictability is neither sufficient nor necessary for defect informativeness. The discriminating experiment should separately estimate both and retain independent pre-dialogue judgments; P critic as written sees the reviewer review (P lines 1205–1213), and P reports only final matched-comment F1 (P lines 270–293, 338–359). In particular, a surface-cue negative control that preserves code semantics could expose shared nuisance signals. Its validity requires human confirmation that the edit preserves defect status.
